text.p: Turkish central bank funded banks via money market operations on Monday due to fresh cash demand although the market opened 26.4 trillion lira long, bankers said.
They said state banks' liquidity needs ahead of hefty mid-month public sector salary payments fuelled demand.
The central bank injected 1.1 trillion lira overnight at 72 percent, 28.6 trillion lira at 67 percent on tmrw/next and 200 billion lira at 68 percent on tmrw/week.
The average overnight money rate leapt to 71.31 percent from 59.31 on Friday when the central bank had drained 9.5 trillion lira at 52 percent overnight, but lent 36.2 trillion lira on t/n and t/w.
"Public sector salary payments are near and there is a continuing liquidity shortage in the market. So we do not expect money rates to go down in the coming days," a banker said.
Bond yields firmed around 1.5 percentage points amid growing concerns over the fate of the Islamist-led coalition government.
"Mounting political uneasiness caused the market to turn to selling. As there are no buyers, bond rates easily go up in thin trade," said a securities manager of a private bank.
The yield on the most heavily traded April 22, 1998 paper ended at 101.52 percent, up from 100.24 on Friday. Volume in other papers were negligible.
The average overnight repo rate dropped to 71.47 percent from Friday's 74.37 percent.
Bankers said the market was irritated by the weekend events, led by the Istanbul protests of about 100,000 demonstrators at a planned clampdown on Islamic schools.

Turkey's powerful secularist army has ordered compulsory secular education be increased to eight years from five as part of measures to fight rising Islamist zeal. This will effectively shut down the middle section of state religious schools.

Former minister Yalim Erez who stepped up his campaign late last week to forge a secularist alliance to replace Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's divided coalition, will hold a second round of talks with opposition leaders this week.

Bankers said the market was also irritated by the Treasury's two-year inflation indexed bond auction set for Tuesday with Wednesday value when the Treasury faces a 78.2 trillion lira worth t-bill redemption.

They said banks needed shorter-term t-bills for their customer portfolios as the inflation-indexed bonds are rarely traded in the secondary market because of their long maturity and some technical problems in pricing.
The lira closed weaker at 136,450 against the dollar due to dollar's surge in the European markets. It had firmed to 136,000 in the morning from Friday's 136,130 close as the dollar sank in Far East.
